pedagogy.summary: At 6-8, interpreting categorical data means USING an organised display to answer questions: read how many in each category, total across all categories, and — the harder step — compare two categories with 'how many more/fewer'. This is Curcio's move from 'reading the data' (lift a value straight off) to 'reading between the data' (combine or compare values). The classic hurdle is that 'how many more' is a DIFFERENCE, not the larger value. Teaching should pose real questions about the child's own chart, model matching/subtracting for comparisons, and keep totals reconciling with the whole group.
bestPractices: Pose a ladder of questions on the child's own display: single-category ('how many chose…'), total ('how many altogether'), then comparison ('how many more… than…')
Model 'how many more' as finding the difference — match the two categories one-to-one and count the gap, or subtract — not reading the taller one
Check the total reconciles with the number of people/objects surveyed as a self-check
Use precise comparison language ('more', 'fewer', 'the difference is') and require the child to say how they got a comparison
keyRepresentations: Frequency table and the child's own pictogram/block diagram as the data source
Two category rows lined up one-to-one to expose the difference
Bar model / number line for the 'how many more' subtraction
A running total check against the full group
commonMisconceptions: Answers 'how many more' with the larger category's value instead of the difference
Finds the total by counting the number of categories rather than summing the frequencies
Reads the wrong value by misaligning a row/column or miscounting
Treats each question in isolation, never checking the total against the whole group

learn.summary: Children aged 6-8 learn to interpret categorical data by using an organised display (their own pictogram, block diagram, or frequency table) to answer a ladder of questions: how many in one category, how many altogether across all categories, and the harder 'how many more/fewer' comparison. The central hurdle is that 'how many more' asks for a DIFFERENCE, not the larger category's value. Activities pose real questions about the child's own survey, model matching/subtracting for comparisons, and keep the running total reconciling with the whole group.

activities.title: Question ladder on your own pets chart
feedback: If a child answers 'how many altogether' with the number of categories (e.g. 4 kinds of pet), return to the data and add the category counts, then check the sum equals the number of children surveyed.

If a child reads a neighbouring category's count or is off by one, steady the reading: track the row across to its count with a finger or ruler. This is a reading lapse to steady, not a concept to reteach.
Prompt 'how did you work out how many more?' to check a difference was computed rather than a value read.
activities.rationale: Curriculum and framework guidance describe interpretation at this age as asking and answering questions about counts, totals and comparisons using an organised display, moving from reading values straight off to combining and comparing them.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils ask and answer questions by counting objects in each category and about totalling and comparing categorical data; Year 3 pupils solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' questions using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables
At Level A the first stage is for students to read and interpret what the data show at a simple level, using the display to answer statistical questions about their group
learnerActions: Collect a small survey (e.g. favourite pet) from your class or family and build it into a pictogram or block diagram.
Answer single-category questions first: 'How many children chose rabbits?' by reading the one row/column.
Answer a total question: 'How many children are there altogether?' by summing ALL the category frequencies, not counting how many kinds of pet there are.
Check your total against the number of people actually surveyed as a self-check.
Answer a comparison question: 'How many more chose dogs than cats?' by finding the difference.
Each time you give a comparison answer, say out loud how you got it.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a single value, totalling all values, and comparing two values are three different moves; the total must reconcile with the whole group, and a comparison asks for a gap between two values.

activities.title: Line them up to see the difference
feedback: If a child gives the taller category's count (8) as the comparison answer, line the two categories up one-to-one, count the unmatched part, and name that 'how many more' means the gap/difference, then re-ask.
To test the comparison on a small gap, ask 'which two categories are closest — how many more does one have than the other?'
A bar model or number line can make the subtraction visible for the 'how many more' step.
activities.rationale: The classic error at this age is answering 'how many more' with the larger value instead of the difference; matching one-to-one and subtracting both make the difference concrete.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils ask and answer questions by counting objects in each category and about totalling and comparing categorical data; Year 3 pupils solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' questions using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables
learnerActions: Pick two categories to compare, e.g. dogs and cats.
Line the two rows up one-to-one so matching items sit directly beside each other.
Count the unmatched part that sticks out on the taller row — that is 'how many more'.
Confirm the same answer by subtracting: taller count minus shorter count (e.g. 8 dogs − 5 cats = 3).
Say the result in comparison words: 'There are 3 more dogs than cats' and 'there are 3 fewer cats than dogs.'
activities.intendedInsight: 'How many more' is the gap between the two categories — the unmatched part — not the height or count of the bigger one.

activities.title: Interactive chart with a comparison tool (optional scaffold)
feedback: If the child relies on the shading to answer, cover it and ask them to find the difference by matching or subtracting themselves.
Use a 'how many more' prompt whose tempting wrong answer is the larger category's raw value, to surface the difference misconception.
activities.rationale: A live display that recolours the gap between two categories may make the comparison concrete and targets the exact place children go wrong; such interactive highlighting is offered here as one supportive scaffold rather than the only route, and its comparative efficacy over a hand-drawn or manipulated display is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Open or build an interactive chart with a question panel under your survey data.
Tap one category and watch its bar light up to answer a single-value question.
Tap two categories (e.g. 'cats' and 'dogs') so the bars glide side by side and the extra squares on the taller bar are shaded as the answer to 'how many more'.
Press a total button that sums the categories and checks the sum equals the number of children surveyed.
After using the tool, redo one comparison and one total by hand to show you can do it without the highlighting.
activities.intendedInsight: Sliding two bars together and shading only the extra squares shows that 'how many more' is the highlighted gap, not the height of the bigger bar; a total button can reconcile the sum with the group size.

activities.title: Combine and reconcile checks
feedback: If the combined total or grand total doesn't match the group, return to the organised data, re-add the category counts, and locate the misread or miscount.
Ask the child to state, in their own words, why the category totals must add up to the whole group.
activities.rationale: Reconciling the running total with the full group is a self-check recommended for this skill and guards against counting categories instead of summing frequencies.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils ask and answer questions by counting objects in each category and about totalling and comparing categorical data; Year 3 pupils solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' questions using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables
learnerActions: Answer 'if the rabbit and cat groups joined, how many would that be?' by adding the two category counts.
Answer 'does your total match how many people you actually surveyed?' and, if not, recount.
Explain why, when each person surveyed gave exactly one answer, the total of all categories should equal the number of people surveyed.
activities.intendedInsight: Categories can be combined by adding their counts, and the sum of all categories should reconcile with the whole surveyed group — a built-in check on your reading.

constraints: Use the child's OWN survey data as the display so the questions are real and the group size is known for the reconcile check.
Use precise comparison language — 'more', 'fewer', 'the difference is' — and require the child to say HOW they reached a comparison; confident numbers alone do not reveal method.
A tap-to-reveal or static chart can surface each category's count for reference but does not require the child to compute a comparison or total; pair it with tasks that demand the computation.

Recognition-only or multiple-choice items can test and give feedback on reading and comparing (including a distractor equal to the larger category's value), but do not by themselves elicit the child independently constructing the difference or total; include construction tasks.
Interactive highlighting of the gap is a scaffold: fade it so the child can match one-to-one or subtract unaided before you treat the skill as secure.
'How many altogether' means summing the frequencies, never counting how many categories there are.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research, re-audited independently without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated conversation and 3D as 'poor' and claimed 3D 'adds nothing' and dialogue 'supplies no data'; these comparative/universal claims are not established by the cited sources and have been dropped. Discussion can still support reasoning about a displayed dataset, and a physical/manipulable layout of the data is a legitimate alternative route.

The interactive comparison tool's sourceClaims are [] because the GAISE 'read and interpret' claim supports interpreting a display but not the efficacy of interactive highlighting; that efficacy remains untested.
Worked example 8 dogs − 5 cats = 3 and the rabbit+cat combine example were checked arithmetically and are correct.

probeDeeper: Ask 'how did you work out how many MORE?' to check a difference was computed, not a value read
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'which two categories are closest — how many between them?' to test the comparison on a small gap
Ask 'does your total match how many children are in our class?' to surface the reconcile check

assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: reads each category value correctly off the display, totals by summing ALL the frequencies (matching the number of children), and answers 'how many more' by finding the difference between the two categories (e.g. 8 dogs − 5 cats = 3), using comparison language.

errorPatterns.pattern: Answers 'how many more chose dogs than cats' with the dogs value (8) instead of the difference (3)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line the two categories up one-to-one and count the unmatched part; name that 'how many more' means the gap/difference, then re-ask
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives the taller category's count as the comparison answer with no subtraction

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds the total by counting the number of categories rather than summing the frequencies
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the organised data: add the category counts and check the sum equals the number of children surveyed
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'how many altogether' with the count of category types (e.g. 4) instead of the sum

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wrong value by misaligning a row/column or miscounting symbols
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with a finger/ruler to track the row across to its count; a reading lapse to steady, not a concept to reteach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reads a neighbouring category's count or is off by one

responseLevels.gap: Reads single values only; gives the larger value for 'how many more' and counts categories for the total
responseLevels.full: Reads all category values, totals by summing frequencies (reconciling with the group), and computes 'how many more/fewer' as a difference, using comparison language independently
responseLevels.partial: Reads values and totals with support, but the comparison is unreliable or done without finding the difference

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is our finished pets chart. Answer these for me: how many children chose rabbits? How many children are there altogether? And how many more chose dogs than cats? (Set the questions and WATCH how each answer is reached.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW each answer is produced is the assessment. A child who understands finds the difference for 'how many more' and sums frequencies for the total; a child who doesn't reports the taller category as 'how many more' and counts categories (getting 'how many kinds') for the total. Both may state numbers confidently — the method is what reveals understanding.
